[[File:Emperor_family_tree0.png|thumb|right|300px|Genealogy from the gods down to Emperor Jimmu and Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime, after the ''Kojiki'']]
'''Himetataraisuzu-hime''' ({{lang|ja|媛蹈鞴五十鈴媛}}){{efn|The ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' writes '''Himetataraisuzu-hime no Mikoto''' ({{lang|ja|媛蹈鞴五十鈴媛命}}). The spelling varies a great deal between sources: {{lang|ja|媛}} and {{lang|ja|姫}}, {{lang|ja|蹈}} and {{lang|ja|踏}}, {{lang|ja|韛}} and {{lang|ja|鞴}}, {{lang|ja|命}} and {{lang|ja|尊}} are all interchanged, giving forms such as {{lang|ja|姫踏鞴五十鈴媛命}}, {{lang|ja|媛蹈韛五十鈴姫尊}}, {{lang|ja|媛蹈韛五十鈴媛命}} and {{lang|ja|姫蹈韛五十鈴姫命}}.}} is a figure and goddess of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', the consort of [[Emperor Jimmu]], the first emperor of Japan, and so the first empress. In the ''[[Kojiki]]'' she corresponds to '''Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime''' ({{lang|ja|比売多多良伊須気余理比売}}).{{efn|The ''Kojiki'' writes '''Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime no Mikoto''' ({{lang|ja|比売多多良伊須気余理比売命}}), Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime, or simply Isukeyori-hime. Sources also vary between {{lang|ja|売}} and {{lang|ja|賣}}, {{lang|ja|気}} and {{lang|ja|氣}}, and {{lang|ja|余}} and {{lang|ja|餘}}.}}

The traditions differ in detail, but all of them make her mother the daughter of a powerful family of the Yamato region and her father a god. She married Jimmu, became empress, and bore the second emperor, [[Emperor Suizei]].

== Other names ==
The ''Kojiki'' says she was first called '''Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime''' ({{lang|ja|富登多多良伊須須岐比売}}, also read Hoto-tatara-isusugi-hime), and that because she disliked the word ''hoto'' ("genitals") the name was later changed to Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime (see [[#The birth story in the Kojiki|the birth story]] below). She is also called simply Isukeyori-hime.

She is sometimes called just '''Isuzu-hime no Mikoto''' ({{lang|ja|五十鈴媛命}}); this should not be confused with her younger sister, [[Isuzuyori-hime]].

== In the Nihon Shoki and Kojiki ==
=== In the Nihon Shoki and Sendai Kuji Hongi ===
She appears as {{lang|ja|姫蹈韛五十鈴姫命}} in book 1 of the ''Nihon Shoki'' (the first part of the Age of the Gods) and in books 4 and 5 of the ''[[Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'', and as {{lang|ja|媛蹈韛五十鈴媛命}} in books 3 (Jimmu) and 4 (Suizei) of the ''Nihon Shoki'' and book 7 of the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi''.

Her parentage is given in several ways:

The daughter, Tataraisuzu-hime no Mikoto, became empress at the court of Kashihara and bore two children, Kamununakawamimi (Emperor Suizei) and Yaimimi.}}

In the alternative account of the Age of the Gods, in the Jimmu and Suizei books, and in the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'', Kotoshironushi visits Tamakushi-hime, daughter of Mizokui of Mishima, and she bears the child. He does so having changed himself into a ''yahiro kuma-wani'', a "great crocodile" or sea monster.

=== In the Kojiki ===
In the middle book of the ''Kojiki'' she appears as Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime no Mikoto and as Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime no Mikoto.

{| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%"
! Source !! Passage !! Mother !! Father !! Notes
|-
| ''Kojiki'' || Middle book, Jimmu || Seyadatara-hime, daughter of Mishima-mizokui || [[Ōmononushi]] || The father is "Ōmononushi of Miwa".{{efn|''Kojiki'': "Here there is a maiden who is called the child of a god. She is called the child of a god because Seyadatara-hime, daughter of Mishima-mizokui, was very beautiful, and Ōmononushi of Miwa saw her and desired her…"}}
|}

Seyadatara-hime was famous for her beauty. Ōmononushi turned himself into an arrow painted red, floated down the stream at the moment she was relieving herself, and struck her genitals (''hoto''). Startled, she picked up the arrow and took it back to her room, where it turned into a handsome young man. The two married and a daughter was born, who was named Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime. The daughter later disliked the word ''hoto'' and changed her name to Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime.

=== Marriage to Jimmu ===
According to the ''Nihon Shoki'' and other sources, Iwarebiko (later Emperor Jimmu) set out east from the land of Himuka,{{efn|Some identify this with [[Hyūga Province]] ([[Miyazaki Prefecture]]); others reject the identification.}} and after many battles established his rule in the Yamato region,{{efn|Generally taken to mean the [[Nara Basin]].}} an episode known as [[Jimmu's Eastern Expedition]]. At the foot of [[Mount Unebi]] he built the palace of Kashihara (in present-day [[Kashihara, Nara]]) and was enthroned as the first emperor.{{efn|Strictly, "Jimmu" is a posthumous name given in the Nara period. The ''Nihon Shoki'' calls him ''Hatsukunishirasu-sumeramikoto'', "the emperor who first ruled the land".}}

Before the enthronement a principal consort fit for the first emperor was sought, and Himetataraisuzu-hime was chosen. The ''Nihon Shoki'' dates their marriage to the 24th day of the 9th month of the year before his accession.{{efn|The ''Nihon Shoki'' has the search for a consort begin on the 16th day of the 8th month of the year before the accession, and the marriage to Himetataraisuzu-hime on the 24th day of the 9th month.}} Jimmu was enthroned in the first month of the following year, and she became empress at that time.{{efn|The ''Nihon Shoki'' places Jimmu's accession in a ''kanoto-tori'' year. Under the calculation fixed in the Meiji period, which drew on the Chinese prophetic theory of revolution in ''kanoto-tori'' years, this becomes 660 BC. It was once treated as historical fact; today it is not generally regarded as history. See [[Japanese imperial year]].}}

The ''Kojiki'' preserves stories about the choice of the consort and the marriage; see [[#Jimmu's courtship|Jimmu's courtship]] below.

=== After Jimmu's death ===
According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', Jimmu died at the age of 127. The ''Nihon Shoki'' and ''Kojiki'' differ in detail, but both describe a fight over the succession among his sons after his death (see [[Tagishimimi]]).

Before leaving Himuka on his expedition, Iwarebiko had married [[Ahiratsu-hime]] and had children by her.{{efn|The ''Kojiki'' names two of them, Tagishimimi and Kisumimi. The ''Nihon Shoki'' names only Tagishimimi and records no one corresponding to Kisumimi.}} When he made Himetataraisuzu-hime his principal consort, these children became children of a lesser wife. After Jimmu's death one of them, Tagishimimi, set out to take the throne himself.{{efn|According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', Tagishimimi had long held office under Jimmu, but had a flawed character and "went against benevolence and righteousness". Such descriptions are not thought to be straightforward history. The succession from Jimmu to Suizei followed ultimogeniture, which may have been usual in early Japan; when primogeniture later became the norm, some suggest, an explanation was needed for readers who took primogeniture to be right, and so the elder brother was cast as a villain who had to be removed.}}

In the ''Kojiki'', Tagishimimi takes the widowed Himetataraisuzu-hime as his own wife and plots to kill the legitimate princes born to her and Jimmu. Sensing this, she composed two poems and sent them to her sons to warn them of the danger.{{efn|''Kojiki'': "After the emperor died, his half-brother Tagishimimi took the empress Isukeyori-hime to wife, and plotted to kill his three younger brothers. Their mother Isukeyori-hime grieved over it, and let her sons know by means of poems."}}

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|狭韋河よ　雲起ちわたり　畝火山　木の葉さやげぬ　風吹かむとす}}
|-
| ''Saikawa yo / kumo tachiwatari / Unebiyama / ko no ha sayagenu / kaze fukamu to su''
|-
| "From the Sai River the clouds are rising; on Mount Unebi the leaves are rustling: the wind is about to blow." Meaning: my children at the house on the Sai River,{{efn|The ''Kojiki'' shows Jimmu visiting Himetataraisuzu-hime's house and staying the night. Some scholars think marriages of the period were visiting marriages, the husband going to the wife's house, and that when an outsider married the daughter of a local power the wife stayed in her family's house and the children were raised there. On this reading Jimmu's legitimate sons were still at their mother's family home on the Sai River when this happened. Scholars do not treat these accounts as history, but as stories reflecting the customs of the time.}} a wind is about to blow towards you from Tagishimimi's side (danger is coming).
|}

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|畝火山　昼は雲と居　夕去れば　風ふかむとぞ　木の葉さやげる}}
|-
| ''Unebiyama / hiru wa kumo to i / yū sareba / kaze fukamu to zo / ko no ha sayageru''
|-
| "Mount Unebi is clouded by day; the leaves rustle, saying that when evening passes the wind will blow."
|}

Learning of Tagishimimi's intended rebellion from these allegorical poems, the legitimate sons struck first and killed him. The one who played the leading part, Kamununakawamimi, took the throne as the second emperor, [[Emperor Suizei]]. According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', Himetataraisuzu-hime took the title of empress dowager (''kōtaigō'') on the 8th day of the 1st month of Suizei's first year.

Suizei took [[Isuzuyori-hime]] as his principal consort. She was Himetataraisuzu-hime's younger sister, and so his aunt. Other traditions differ: one makes his consort Kawamata-bime, and another makes his empress Itoori-hime.

=== Children ===
Her children by Jimmu, eldest first, were [[Hikoyai]], [[Kamuyaimimi]], and Kamununakawamimi ([[Emperor Suizei]]).

=== Siblings ===
Her mother, Tamakushi-hime (Seyadatara-hime), is said to have borne two other children:
* {{ill|Amenohikatakushihikata|ja|天日方奇日方命}}, her elder brother. The ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' says he served Jimmu and became chief minister.
* [[Isuzuyori-hime]], her younger sister, later consort of the second emperor, Suizei.

== Theories about her origin ==
The ''Nihon Shoki'' and ''Kojiki'' differ in detail, but both give Himetataraisuzu-hime a mother who is the daughter of a local power (a god) and a father who is a god. One interpretation is that by taking "the daughter of a god" as his principal wife, the first emperor was securing the legitimacy of his rule.

Her mother's side is placed at Mishima in [[Settsu Province|Settsu]] (Osaka Prefecture) and her father's side at Miwa ([[Mount Miwa]]) in [[Yamato Province|Yamato]] (Nara Prefecture). This points to the cooperation of several clans of the Kinki region,{{efn|If, as the ''Nihon Shoki'' says, her father was Kotoshironushi or Ōkuninushi, she also had roots in the [[Izumo]] region, in addition to the clans of Kinki.}} and some read the marriage as showing that the powers of the Yamato and Settsu region{{efn|Strictly, provinces such as Yamato and Settsu were established later, in the ancient ''ritsuryō'' system.}} supported Iwarebiko, an outsider who had come from Himuka. Others read it as a political method: rather than relying on conquest alone, Iwarebiko secured his base by marrying into the local powers. Another reading, discussed below, takes it as a sign that Jimmu's following gained control of ironmaking.

=== Grandfather: Mizokui of Mishima ===
The ''Nihon Shoki'' makes her mother the daughter of '''Mishima-mizokui''', with slight differences of wording. The name is written in several ways: {{lang|ja|溝樴}}, {{lang|ja|溝樴耳神}}, {{lang|ja|溝杙}}; the ''Kojiki'' has {{lang|ja|湟咋}}, and the ''[[Shinsen Shōjiroku]]'' {{lang|ja|溝杭}}. Since some sources add the divine suffix ''-mimi no kami'', one view holds that he was worshipped as a god.{{efn|The jawiki source adds, with a verification request, that this god is identified with Suetsumimi, Kamo-taketsunumi and [[Yatagarasu]], and that the genealogies of the [[Kamo clan]] make him the ancestral god of the Kamo clan and of the Kazuraki ''kuni no miyatsuko''.}}

Mishima is thought to be [[Mishima District, Osaka|Mishima District]] of Settsu Province, in the north of present-day Osaka Prefecture. The ''[[Engishiki]] Jinmyōchō'' (927) lists the [[Mishima Kamo Shrine]] (Mishimae, [[Takatsuki]]) and the {{ill|Mizokui Shrine|ja|溝咋神社}} ([[Ibaraki, Osaka|Ibaraki]]), and "Mizokui of Mishima" is thought to have been a local land god worshipped in this area.{{efn|The Mizokui Shrine regards Mishima-mizokui as its founding ancestor, and the Mishima clan is thought to have been a powerful clan of ancient Kawachi.}}

The Edo-period ''kokugaku'' scholar [[Motoori Norinaga]] took ''mizo'' ("ditch") to mean a privy built over running water, and this became the accepted reading. Mitani Eiichi and others follow it, and one theory connects privies with childbirth ritual. Higo Kazuo, professor emeritus of Tokyo University of Education, read ''mizo'' instead as the ditches of rice fields; Tsugita Masaki developed this, arguing that Mishima District was well suited to rice growing and that "Mizokui of Mishima" was an agricultural god.

=== Mother: Tamakushi-hime and Seyadatara-hime ===
The ''Nihon Shoki'' calls her mother [[Tamakushi-hime]] and the ''Kojiki'' Seyadatara-hime. Both say she was famous for her surpassing beauty.{{efn|''Nihon Shoki'': "She was the finest beauty in the land." ''Kojiki'': "Her appearance was beautiful."}}

Motoori Norinaga identified the ''Seya'' of the ''Kojiki'' with Seno village in Heguri District, Yamato Province (now [[Sangō, Nara|Sangō]], [[Ikoma District, Nara|Ikoma District]], Nara Prefecture).

=== Birth through a divine marriage ===
In both the ''Nihon Shoki'' and the ''Kojiki'' her birth comes from a marriage between a woman and a being of another kind. Her father visits her mother in a changed form: a ''yahiro wani'' in the ''Nihon Shoki'', a red-painted arrow in the ''Kojiki''. She is therefore known as the leading example in Japanese myth of a child born of such a marriage.{{efn|Jimmu's own father, [[Ugayafukiaezu]], was born to [[Toyotama-hime]], whose true form was a ''yahiro wani''. His father [[Hoori]] did not know this, spied on the birth, and saw her true form, so Toyotama-hime left the newborn and returned to the sea. That child was Jimmu's father.}}

=== The birth story in the Kojiki ===
The ''Kojiki'' makes her the daughter of [[Ōmononushi]].{{efn|Ōmononushi was originally the clan god of the Miwa clan. He is also sometimes treated as another name of [[Ōkuninushi]], a descendant of [[Susanoo]], and the ''Nihon Shoki'' makes Ōmononushi Ōkuninushi's ''nigimitama'' (gentle spirit). The two are thought to have been separate gods originally.}} Her home was Miwa, or Mount Miwa in the Yamato region.

{| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%"
|-
| Original || {{lang|ja|美和之大物主神見感而、其美人爲大便之時、化丹塗矢、自其爲大便之溝流下、突其美人之富登。}}
|-
| Meaning || Ōmononushi of Miwa saw the beautiful Seyadatara-hime and desired her. He turned himself into a red-painted arrow, and at the time she came to relieve herself he floated down the stream and struck her ''hoto''.
|}

{| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%"
|-
| Original || {{lang|ja|爾其美人驚而、立走伊須須岐伎、乃將來其矢、置於床邊、忽成麗壯夫、卽娶其美人生子}}
|-
| Meaning || Startled, Seyadatara-hime jumped up and ran about, then took the arrow back to her room and laid it by her bed, where it at once became a handsome young man. He married her, and she bore a child.
|}

From the way she came to be born, the child was named '''Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime''', taken to mean "the child born when [her mother] was struck in the ''hoto'' and was startled". Like her mother, she is said to have been beautiful.

She herself disliked ''hoto'', however, and changed her name to '''Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime'''.

=== Theories about the name ===
The original name ''Hoto-tatara'' comes from the story of her mother being struck in the genitals by the arrow. One reading takes ''tatara'' as a derivative of ''tatsu'', "to stand", as in "the ''hoto'' stood"; the name was later changed from ''hoto'' to ''hime''. Another theory has ''tatara'' inherited from part of her mother's name, Seyadatara-hime. ''Isusuki'' is said to mean "to be startled and run off", and ''isuke'' to be a rewording of it.

Another reading connects ''tatara'' with ironmaking, and holds that Jimmu's marriage to her symbolises the state gaining control of iron smelting, an important technology of the time; see [[#Connection with tatara ironmaking|below]].

''Isuzu'' ({{lang|ja|五十鈴}}, "fifty bells") is said by some to mean bells, referring to someone whose hands and feet were adorned with many bells, and by others to point to metalworking (the casting of bells). Yet another view holds that the original ''isusuki'' was corrupted into ''isuzu''.

''Yori'' has been read as ''yoroshi'', "good", and also as related to ''yuri'', the lily, referring to the ''sasayuri'' lilies (''[[Lilium japonicum]]'') that grow on the banks of the [[Sai River (Nara)|Sai River]] at the foot of Mount Miwa, where her family's house stood.

== Jimmu's courtship ==
Before his enthronement Jimmu was to take a principal consort fit for the first emperor. [[Ōkume]], a retainer who had followed Iwarebiko from Himuka, put forward Isukeyori-hime (Himetataraisuzu-hime) as a candidate. In the ''Kojiki'' Ōkume tells Jimmu the story of her birth and argues that Isukeyori-hime, as "the child of a god", is worthy to be his empress.

The ''Kojiki'' tells how Jimmu and Ōkume saw seven women on the banks of the Sai River and chose the empress from among them. The poems exchanged on this occasion between Jimmu, Ōkume and Isukeyori-hime are well known as Jimmu's courtship story (''tsumadoi setsuwa'').

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|倭の高佐士野を七行く媛女ども誰をしまかむ}}
|-
| ''Yamato no / Takasajinu o / nana yuku / otomedomo / tare o shi makamu''
|-
| "Of the seven maidens walking on Takasajinu in Yamato, which shall I take as my wife?"
|}

Takasajinu is the terrace along the Sai River. The Sai is a small stream rising on Mount Miwa and flowing near the grounds of [[Ōmiwa Shrine]]; before joining the [[Yamato River]] (Hatsuse River) it becomes a raised-bed river with high banks.

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|かつがつも　いや先立てる　兄をしまかむ}}
|-
| ''Katsugatsu mo / iya sakidateru / e o shi makamu''
|-
| "I will take the eldest, the one walking in front" (Isukeyori-hime).
|}

At Jimmu's wish Ōkume went to meet Isukeyori-hime. Surprised by his unfamiliar appearance, she answered:

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|天地 千鳥真鵐　など黥ける利目}}
|-
| ''Ametsutsu / chidori mashitoto / nado sakeru tome''
|-
| "Why are your eyes tattooed round like those of so many birds, and why is your gaze so sharp?"
|}

Ōkume replied:

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|媛女に　直に逢わんと　我が黥ける利目}}
|-
| ''Otome ni / tada ni awamu to / waga sakeru tome''
|-
| "My eyes are sharp so that I can see you directly, maiden."
|}

Isukeyori-hime then agreed to the marriage. Jimmu went to her house "above the Sai River" and spent a night there, which is described in the poem:

{| style="background-color:WhiteSmoke;padding:10px;"
|-
| {{lang|ja|葦原の　穢しき小屋に　菅畳　いや清敷きて　我が二人寝し}}
|-
| ''Ashihara no / shikeshiki oya ni / sugatatami / iya sayashikite / waga futari neshi''
|-
| "In a humble hut among the reeds, we spread clean sedge mats and the two of us slept."
|}

A note at this point explains the name of the Sai River: many ''yamayurigusa'' (in fact ''sasayuri'') grew there, and since another name for this lily is ''sai'', the river was called the Sai River. A monument to Jimmu at the Sai River now stands on its right bank.

== Connection with tatara ironmaking ==
One theory links the ''tatara'' in her name with [[tatara]] ironmaking and takes it as evidence of iron smelting in ancient Japan.{{efn|The character {{lang|ja|鞴}} used to write her name in the ''Nihon Shoki'' means the bellows used in ironmaking.}}{{efn|Before the end of the Second World War it was held that ironmaking in Japan went back to the Age of the Gods. The ''Nihon Shoki'' and ''Kojiki'' tell how, when [[Amaterasu]] hid in the [[Ama-no-Iwato|heavenly rock cave]], metal was worked using iron from Mount Ama-no-Kagu (''Nihon Shoki'') or Ama-no-Kanayama (''Kojiki''). Today ironmaking is generally thought to have come from the Chinese mainland together with rice farming, but the archaeological evidence is thin and there is no settled view of its origin or date. In the written record, ironmaking is described in detail in the eighth-century ''[[Izumo no Kuni Fudoki]]'' and is thought to have been established by then.}}{{efn|Suzumoto Teiichi of the Chemical Society of Japan argued that the huge [[Daisen Kofun|tomb of Emperor Nintoku]], dated to the early fifth century, could only have been built with established iron tools, and that the Yamato court of the time must have commanded tatara ironmaking. Bellows have been excavated at the Higashi-Nara site ([[Ibaraki, Osaka|Ibaraki]], Osaka), and some connect this with ironmaking by the Yamato court. The site, found in 1971, has also yielded [[dōtaku]] bronze bells and their moulds, and the bells were certainly made there.}}

According to Konoda Yasunao of Nara Women's University, ''tatara'' is the tatara furnace, and ''hoto'' means both genitals and the hearth of a furnace.{{efn|''Hoto'' has also been taken to mean a smelting furnace.}} Jimmu's taking Himetataraisuzu-hime (Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime, Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime) as his wife is then read as the royal house taking control of the iron industry. Yoshino Yutaka of the Japanese Literature Association took the name Hoto-tatara-isukeyori-hime to mean a goddess of smelting, or a shrine maiden serving the furnace.

The early modern ''kokugaku'' scholars, beginning with Motoori Norinaga, did not read ''tatara'' as "bellows". In their view ''tatara'' was smiths' slang, unfit for the name of a noble empress, and so they rejected the link with ironmaking. They read ''tatara'' as a derivative of ''tatsu'', meaning "stood up (startled at being struck in the genitals)" or "had an arrow stood (in the genitals)".

== Worship ==
At [[Kashihara Shrine]], founded by [[Emperor Meiji]] in 1890, Jimmu and Himetataraisuzu-hime are enshrined as the principal deities.

Because she saved her children, Himetataraisuzu-hime came to be revered as a guardian deity of children (''Komori Myōjin''), and she is the principal deity of {{ill|Isagawa Shrine|ja|率川神社}} (Honkomori-chō, Nara).{{efn|Isagawa Shrine is a subsidiary shrine of [[Ōmiwa Shrine]], at Mount Miwa, said to be her home.}} Every June the shrine holds the Saikusa Festival, popularly the Lily Festival, at which ''sasayuri'' grown on Mount Miwa are offered to her.

At Miwa, [[Sakurai, Nara|Sakurai]], Nara Prefecture, on the upper reaches of the Sai River where her family's house is said to have stood, is Sai Shrine. Its principal deity is the ''aramitama'' (rough spirit) of the god of Ōmiwa, and it also enshrines Himetataraisuzu-hime, [[Ōmononushi]] (her father in the ''Kojiki''), Seyadatara-hime (her mother in the ''Kojiki'') and [[Kotoshironushi]] (her father in the ''Nihon Shoki'').

She is also enshrined at Tsumori Jingū ([[Mashiki, Kumamoto|Mashiki]], Kamimashiki District, Kumamoto Prefecture) and at Kōsa Shrine ([[Kōsa, Kumamoto|Kōsa]], Kamimashiki District).
